tagline: Down a stocked trout stream on gravel forest roads.
intro: Known locally as the Williams River Road, the backway starts near the river's headwaters in Pocahontas County and follows it down on narrow gravel forest roads 86 and 216 to its meeting with the Gauley near Cowen. The water runs over a rocky, boulder-strewn bed between densely forested hills.

This country was heavily logged early in the 20th century and has grown back since. The river is stocked with some 27,000 pounds of trout a year, and about 30 rustic campsites line the road, many of them close to the water.
season: The West Virginia Byways and Backways guide says the road is drivable from spring through fall, and that spring and fall are the most popular seasons for anglers.

moments.title: Tea Creek
moments.text: The creek was named for water stained brown like tea, and its campground is one of two the state guide names on the river, with numerous primitive sites besides.

moments.title: Cranberry Wilderness
moments.text: Trails lead from the road into the Cranberry Wilderness, a designated black bear sanctuary, which the river leaves at Three Forks, its lowest ground at 2,400 feet.

moments.title: Dyer
moments.text: The village was called Haynes until 1911, when it took the name of George M. Dyer, who had been its postmaster since 1893 and stayed on until 1923.

practical: Narrow gravel forest roads, not maintained through the winter months. RVs should proceed with caution.
